plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the geometry of light refraction at a planar interface between two optical media, as described by Snell's law. A horizontal black line divides the scene into an upper region with refractive index n1 and a lower region with refractive index n2; a thick blue line traces the ray direction as it strikes the interface and continues into the second medium. A thin vertical line marks the surface normal at the point of incidence, with a small right-angle square confirming its perpendicularity to the interface; the angle theta_1 is measured between the incoming ray and the normal above the interface, and theta_2 is measured between the refracted ray and the normal below. The ray bends toward or away from the normal depending on the relative magnitudes of n1 and n2, embodying the relationship n1 sin theta_1 = n2 sin theta_2. This figure introduces refraction geometry as the physical basis for how lenses bend light and form images.

interactionPlan.concept: Light bends at the boundary between two media according to the ratio of their refractive indices (Snell's law), and undergoes total internal reflection if refracting into a lower-index medium is geometrically impossible.
elements: Horizontal black line representing the interface between media
Thin blue vertical line representing the surface normal, labeled 'surface normal'
Small right-angle square marker at the intersection of the interface and normal
Thick blue line in the upper half representing the incident ray, labeled 'ray direction'
Thick blue line in the lower half representing the refracted ray
Thick blue line in the upper half representing the reflected ray (appears only during total internal reflection)
Arc and text label 'θ₁' between the incident ray and upper normal
Arc and text label 'θ₂' between the refracted ray and lower normal
Text label 'n₁' in the upper medium
Text label 'n₂' in the lower medium

interactions.label: Incident angle (θ₁)
interactions.teaches: Changing the angle of incidence smoothly changes the angle of refraction according to the trigonometric relationship of Snell's law.

interactions.label: Refractive index n₁ (upper)
interactions.teaches: Increasing the density of the first medium relative to the second makes the ray bend further away from the normal in the second medium.

interactions.label: Refractive index n₂ (lower)
interactions.teaches: Increasing the density of the second medium causes the refracted ray to bend closer to the surface normal.

demo_steps.title: Entering a denser medium
demo_steps.narration: When light passes from a lower-index medium (like air, n₁=1.0) to a higher-index medium (like glass, n₂=1.5), it bends toward the surface normal (θ₂ < θ₁).

demo_steps.title: Entering a less dense medium
demo_steps.narration: If light travels from a higher-index to a lower-index medium, it bends away from the normal (θ₂ > θ₁). Notice how much wider the refracted angle becomes.

demo_steps.title: Total Internal Reflection
demo_steps.narration: If moving to a lower-index medium at a steep enough angle, refraction becomes impossible (sin θ₂ > 1). The light is completely reflected back into the first medium.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The direction light bends depends entirely on the ratio of the refractive indices, and total internal reflection occurs when bending away from the normal reaches a physical limit.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: 2D geometric diagram. The interface is a solid horizontal black line; the normal is a thin light-blue vertical line. Rays are thick, darker blue lines. Mathematically bind the refracted ray angle θ₂ to arcsin((n₁/n₂) * sin(θ₁)). When (n₁/n₂) * sin(θ₁) > 1, hide the refracted ray and its θ₂ arc, and instead draw a reflected ray in the upper medium mirrored across the normal at angle θ₁. Keep the n₁ and n₂ labels prominently floating in their respective halves.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Drag the incident ray to change θ₁ and watch θ₂ update in real time according to n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, with both angle arc labels refreshing as the ray rotates about the interface point
- Sliders for refractive indices n₁ and n₂: show how increasing n₂ relative to n₁ bends the refracted ray closer to the surface normal, and vice versa
- Increase n₁ above n₂ and drag θ₁ past the critical angle to trigger total internal reflection, showing the refracted ray disappear below the interface and a reflected ray appear symmetrically above it
